70476.etyen:
Partial calque of English spot trade. Compound of spot (“spot; for immediate delivery”) + handel (“trade, trading”), literally “spot trade”.
The first element, spot (“spot; for immediate delivery”), is borrowed from English spot (“spot; for immediate delivery”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *(s)pel- (“to split”).
The final element, handel (“trade, trading”), is from Middle Low German handel (“trade, commerce”), a verbal noun of handelen (“to act, trade”), ultimately related to hand (“hand”) and Proto-Germanic *handuz (“hand”), of uncertain further origin.

1000524.etyen: The uppercase form of s. From Latin S, through Etruscan 𐌔 (s), from a western form of Ancient Greek Σ (S, “sigma”), ultimately from Phoenician 𐤔 (š, “šīn; tooth”). The shape and alphabetic position of Greek sigma continue Phoenician šīn, whose sibilant sound was adapted to Greek /s/. The Greek name σίγμα (sígma, “sigma”) may have been influenced by Phoenician 𐤎 (s, “sāmek”), while the latter letter otherwise developed into Greek Ξ (X, “xi”). 1005132.etyen:
From fiss (“F-sharp”) + -iss (“semitone-raising suffix”), literally “F-sharp-sharp”. The base fiss (“F-sharp”) is itself formed from f (“the note F”) and -iss (“semitone-raising suffix; sharp”). The suffix -iss is from German -is (“semitone-raising suffix; sharp”).
Compare the parallel formations Danish fisis, Swedish fississ, German Fisis, Dutch fisis and Finnish fisis (“F double sharp”).
